drills.q: Which of Claude Code and Codex leads Terminal-Bench 2.0, and by roughly how much (as of 2026-08-01)?
Which tool wins blind pairwise code-cleanliness review, and roughly how often?
drills.a: Claude Code, roughly 67% of the time.

drills.q: Why can't Cursor run headless in CI?
drills.a: It's an IDE -- the interaction model assumes a human watching diffs. This is architectural, not a settings gap.

drills.q: Is Microsoft Agent Framework a fourth finished coding agent competing with Claude Code/Codex/Cursor?
drills.a: No -- it's an SDK for building a harness, one level down the stack; it competes with hand-rolling your own loop.

drills.q: What's the Agent Framework gotcha that silently kills long sessions?
drills.a: Compaction is disabled unless BOTH MaxContextWindowTokens and MaxOutputTokens are supplied, with no error on omission.

drills.q: What Claude Code permission mechanism does NOT fire in headless (-p) mode, and what replaces it?
drills.a: PermissionRequest hooks don't fire; enforcement must be re-derived via PreToolUse hooks or --allowedTools.

drills.q: Distinguish model lock-in from workflow lock-in for Cursor specifically.
drills.a: Low model lock-in (BYO API key reaches Claude/GPT/Gemini); high workflow/IDE lock-in (extensions, keybindings, muscle memory are Cursor-specific).

drills.q: What's the difference between 'configuration control' and 'implementation control' over an agent loop, and which tools offer implementation control?
drills.a: Configuration control tunes an existing loop (hooks, permission rules -- all three finished products). Implementation control means rewriting the loop itself -- only Agent Framework or hand-rolling.

drills.q: A team needs an agent's permission decisions to consult an internal compliance policy service per call. Which tool fits and why do the other three fall short?
drills.a: Agent Framework -- it needs implementation control over the permission engine, which none of the three finished products expose past fixed hooks or diff-accept UIs.

drills.q: Why should a hard requirement like headless CI disqualify a tool rather than just lower its average score?
drills.a: A tool great on 8 axes but structurally unable to meet a required 9th is disqualified, not '8/9 good' -- averaging hides an architectural gap that surfaces later as a costly switch.

drills.q: Why does this module explicitly warn that its own cited benchmark numbers will be stale?
drills.a: Four vendors ship monthly; any specific score is a snapshot. The nine evaluation axes are durable; the numbers on them are not.

drills.q: Does picking the 'best' harness substitute for code review discipline?
drills.a: No -- harness choice affects speed and cleanliness of generation, not whether architecture and review are sound. Weak review produces bad outcomes on any of the four, just at different speed.
